title: The Birds That Cross the World
text:
Every autumn, a small wading bird called the bar-tailed godwit lifts off from the mudflats of Alaska and points itself south. It does not stop. It does not eat. It does not land on water, because it cannot swim.
Eleven thousand kilometres and nine days later, it drops out of the sky over New Zealand, having lost half its body weight in flight.
Before leaving, the bird prepares in a way that seems almost deliberate. It eats until it is grotesquely fat, and then its internal organs shrink — the stomach and liver reduce in size, because on a journey with no meals, they are simply weight worth carrying less of.
Nobody teaches it the route. A young godwit making the crossing for the first time flies alone, navigating by stars and wind and something we still do not fully understand.
We have known about this journey for barely twenty years. It has been happening for millions.
